title: Not Yes or No
concept: The Fairbanks Daily News-Miner (October 18th), the Anchorage Daily News (October 22nd) and the Alaska Beacon (September 18th and October 24th) report how Alaska's legislative and governor candidates answer the data center question, and that the Senate passed a data center bill 14 to 5 that the House never took up. A steel-blue ballot box with a face, the BallotBox, spits out a YES / NO slip whose boxes melt into three sliding rails, SIZE, PLACE and WHO PAYS. The film follows the slip across a forum stage of twelve podiums, an IN tray, a padlocked gate that a STUDY key opens, a cash register and a coin envelope, a painted map with a shed and a huge hall, a governor stage, a limit line at hyperscale, a sagging power pole, a counter bell, one green line that plugs two rival buildings in, the bill sheet flipping to SENATE 14 TO 5, a session bell, and a blank FIRST RULE UNWRITTEN sheet that the BallotBox swallows before spitting out the opening slip.

fingerprint.palette: pale sage hall walls, honey gym floor, cranberry booth curtains and flag, steel box with a parchment slip, ink-black rails, aurora lamps for electricity only
fingerprint.metaphor: a yes or no ballot slip whose boxes melt into three sliding rails: size, place and who pays

palette: pale sage hall walls, honey gym floor, cranberry booth curtains and flag, steel box with a parchment slip, ink-black rails, aurora lamps for electricity only
divergence_note: The last films were a rain boardwalk of signs (10-25), a navy orbit (10-24), a paper building in snow (10-23) and a dark tundra bob (10-22). This film is a bright indoor civic hall in sage and honey with a cranberry accent and aurora green for electricity only, built of a ballot slip, sliders, podiums, a padlocked gate and an IN tray. There is no rain, no sign hero, no orbit, no cutaway ground, no paper creature, no remote, no pause button and no calendar. HONEST OVERLAP: its hero is a faced object for the fifth film in a row, but it is a hard steel box with a slot mouth and a flag.

treatment.winner: The Explainer's ballot slip that melts into three rails, with the Enthusiast's face-down bill sheet in the IN tray as the primary loop, the Dramatist's unplugged power cord as the secondary loop, and the Comedian's coin gag. The pause is a padlocked gate with a key, never a button.
treatment.why: All four pitches converged on a YES / NO slip that becomes sliders. The thesis is that the argument is size, place and who pays, so the picture is a slip whose boxes melt into three rails, and the unfinished bill is the sheet that sat in the tray.

angle.thesis: Alaska's candidates mostly aren't arguing yes or no on data centers, they're arguing size, place and who pays, and the one bill that wrote those terms passed the Senate 14 to 5 and then went untouched by the House, so the people elected on November 3rd write Alaska's first data center rule.
angle.falsifiable_by: A covered candidate who opposes data centers of any size anywhere with no condition; or moratorium backers who want a permanent ban rather than a pause until a study or framework; or the Senate bill proving to be a yes/no permission vote rather than rules on utility power and decommissioning; or a data center framework already in force; or no similar bill filed next session.
supporting_facts: c3 12 Fairbanks area candidates generally agreed big data centers need rules and local input (News-Miner)
c5/c16 the moratoriums are conditional pauses that end when a study or framework exists
c10/c11/c12 one South Anchorage race: modest and purpose built vs large on the North Slope, and both see energy investment
c6/c7/c8/c9 tax, digital dividend, grid readiness, local zoning are answers about who pays and who decides
c17/c18/c19 the Senate passed 14 to 5 a bill on utility power use and decommissioning plans, the House never took it up
angle.counterpoint_honored: Rules first costs a candidate nothing, a moratorium works like a no in practice, Bronson and Taylor said unqualified yes in September (c13/c14), Tomaszewski says the grid isn't ready (c8), and Prax and Haney say the first rule belongs to local government (c9). Act three gives the pause-and-grid side and the borough-zoning side a scene at full strength, then the open question whether Juneau or the borough writes the first word.
angle.second_movement: c19 + c18: the bill that got furthest was an electricity and decommissioning bill, so the data center question is really a power-bill and cleanup question, and the unfinished bill is the framework both the moratorium camp (c16) and the build camp wait for.
angle.throughline_object: THE BALLOT SLIP. States: (1) two-box YES/NO slip, (2) the boxes melt into three sliders SIZE / PLACE / WHO PAYS, (3) each slider set differently per candidate, (4) the slip becomes the Senate bill sheet stamped 14 to 5 and parked in an IN tray, (5) a blank rule sheet with a pen hovering, FIRST RULE UNWRITTEN.
angle.hero: BallotBox (net-new reusable hero: a steel ballot box with a slot mouth, a face and a flag)
angle.ai_link_wording: The data center is the machine room AI runs in. The candidates talk about data centers, the Beacon and ADN stories don't say AI throughout, so the film says data centers and AI's compute, never an AI bill.
angle.valence: Constructive, Alaska-first, even-handed. No villain, no savior. The House stall is a calendar fact.
angle.one_question: Which of the three decides your yes, the size, the place or who pays for the power?
runner_ups: Rule-writer only (who writes the first rule): folded in as the Act 4 button
Enthusiast upside: folded in as c12 shared ground and the dividend/tax scenes
Sullivan/RPM conflict: lost, single partisan source
